newsitem.title: UK: UK regulator puts forward plans for new watchdog.
newsitem.headline: UK regulator puts forward plans for new watchdog.

text.p: Britain's new enlarged financial watchdog is to take over responsibility for supervision of the banking industry in the first half of 1998, according to proposals published on Thursday.

The second phase of the plan outlined in a report to Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown from outgoing SIB chairman Andrew Large will see staff of the self regulatory organisations (SROs) transfer to the new regulator also next year.

The new regulator, initially dubbed 'super-SIB' but now referred to by officials as NewRO (New Regulatory Organisation), will bring together the regulatory powers of the Bank of England, the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) and (SROs) under one roof.
The SROs will continue as legal regulators of their member firms until complete integration in late 1999 or early 2000.
The nine current bodies cover banking; insurance; building societies; the investment management industry; retail investments; and securities and futures trading.

SIB, Bank of England and SRO staff will all come under single employment contracts early next year. NewRO will have around 2,000 staff, broadly in line with current numbers across the different regulatory bodies.
It is currently looking for premises including the City - London's main financial centre - and the Docklands on its outskirts.
There is likely to be at least one regional office, in Edinburgh.
New SIB chief Howard Davies said all nine bodies were committed to ensuring that the transition was as smooth and efficient as possible.
The new regulator will take a risk-based approach to supervision reflecting the nature of the business activities concerned and the relative sophistication of the consumers involved.
It will look to the senior management of regulated firms to ensure compliance.

The report outlines a draft structure including Authorisation; Supervision; and Policy Formulation departments and suggests ways of ensuring greater accountability including an external appeals system, a dedicated quality control unit and more appearances by officials before the Treasury Select Committee.
The process of integrating regulation, including for the first time the supervision and surveillance of banks, was put forward by Brown in May.
It reflects the changes that have taken place across the financial services industry as distinctions between for example investment and retail banks and insurers have broken down.
Formal consultations on the proposals are envisaged to begin in October.
One important issue to be resolved will be the funding of the new body by the industry.

The Bank of England Bill, integrating the Bank's supervisory functions with the SIB, will be presented to Parliament in the autumn. This will be followed by a draft bill to bring about full integration which will be published in the summer of 1998.
Before then, a process of extensive consultation will continue with questions including those of funding arrangements, compensation, ombudsman schemes and practitioner and consumer involvement.
